newsitem.title: TURKEY: FEATURE - Turkish Islamic banks seek legal changes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Turkish Islamic banks seek legal changes.

text.p: Islamic banks are keen to win a larger share of Turkey's financial business but are hampered by regulations they say are unjust and discriminatory.
The banks satisfy a demand from a significant part of society which never invests in interest-bearing saving instruments because of religious concerns, their officials say.
But they pay higher taxes than non-Islamic banks. Once freed from inequalities, they foresee rapid growth of their small share of the market.

"It is not the time to earn money from money. We use our customers' savings in trading or project financing. If we are given more rights, that will improve trade and the economy in the country at the same time," said Hikmet Guler, general manager at Saudi-owned Faisal Finance.

"There is money which is not going to the banking system in Turkey. This is a reality. We collect this money and support trading operations in Turkey by using it," Mehmet Savas, general manager at Ihlas Finans, told Reuters.
Five Islamic financial institutions operate in predominantly Moslem, but secular Turkey. They have only a three percent stake in the whole financial system which embraces about 70 banks.
Orthodox Islamic jurists say the ban on "riba" (usury), which is explicit in the Koran, applies to all fixed interest loans.

Islamic banks pay a profit share to their customers in return for their savings. They also provide some other banking services which do not bear interest -- such as sight deposits and foreign currency deposits and foreign exchange and trade transactions.
Clients of Turkish commercial banks pay a five percent "banking and insurance transaction tax" while there is a 10 percent withholding tax on Islamic banks' profit sharing.

"(Islamic) Financial institutions' growth was not as fast as it was expected. Because there are some legal problems. When the banking law was prepared, there were no (Islamic) financial institutions in Turkey. So we can not operate in the gold and stock market. That curbs our growth," Guler of Faisal Finans said.
Turkey's Capital Market Board licences banks and brokerage houses only to act as intermediaries on Istanbul's stock and gold exchanges.

However Turkish bankers say Islamic financial institutions have some advantageous -- lower reserve requirement and liquidity ratios and an exemption from a foreign exchange risk ratio which banks must attain.
Islamic bankers have become more optimistic about positive government action since the new coalition government led by the Islamist Welfare Party's Necmettin Erbakan took office in early July.

Among the five Islamic financial institutions in Turkey, only Ihlas Finans Kurumu, owned by Ihlas Holding, is listed on the Istanbul Stock Exchange. The company, founded last year, offered 15 percent of its capital to the public in April.
Savas said Ihlas' offer to the public was a major factor behind its rapid growth.
Ihlas Finans distributed an annual profit share of 104 percent in July. One-year bank deposits earned around 100 percent in the same period. Annual inflation is running at about 80 percent.
According to Turkish law, Islamic banks can retain 20 percent of their total profits for their salary and tax costs and pay the remaining 80 percent to customers in the form of a profit share.
Like other banks, Islamist banks offer profit shares at various maturities from one month to one year.
"There might be similarities between interest rates and profit share. But that does not mean that there are similarities operationally," Guler said.

"Since we live in the same country, we should take into account the same parameters -- inflation, exchange rates and interest rates -- when we make our calculations. We see interest rates as a parameter but not as a system."
